questions.stem: What is the finding of the AAA survey?
options: A) The majority of drivers prefer to drive and park themselves.
B) Human drivers become easily distracted or tired while driving.
C) Most drivers feel uncertain about the safety of self-driving cars.
D) Most drivers have test driven cars with automatic braking features.

explain.定位:
But 75% of drivers say they wouldn't feel safe in such a vehicle.
但有 75% 的司机表示，他们坐这种（自动驾驶）车时不会感到安全。
explain.信号:
转折 But + 百分比数字双信号。这句以转折词 But 起头，紧接一个醒目的百分比 75% of
drivers，转折后才是真意、数字又是新闻高频考点，双重信号叠加，这句就是承载『调查发
现』的答案句。
explain.替换:
75% of drivers ↔ Most drivers
75% 概括为『大多数』
wouldn't feel safe ↔ feel uncertain about the safety
『不觉得安全』改写为『对安全没把握』
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
A 借用了录音里 self-parking、drive 这类词造出 prefer to drive and park themselves
（更愿自己开自己停），听着耳熟；但原文第三段说司机『相信自己的驾驶技术』，并没说
『更愿自己开自己停车』，这是把后文一句的意思偷换、且并非本题问的『调查发现』。
借用原文：self-parking the next time they buy a new car
B) 张冠李戴
distracted or tired 直接搬了原文第二段 they wouldn't get distracted or drive when
tired 的原词，但那是『自动驾驶支持者』论证无人车更安全时说的，说的是车不会分心疲
劳，不是调查发现『人类司机易分心疲劳』，主语和出处都被偷换了。
借用原文：they wouldn't get distracted or drive when tired
D) 原词陷阱
test driven cars with automatic braking features 拼用了录音里的 automatic braking
（自动刹车）这一原词，但原文只说 60% 司机『想要』自动刹车等功能、是 want 不是
have test driven（试驾过），调查里根本没说大多数司机试驾过，属无中生有。
借用原文：such as automatic braking or self-parking

questions.stem: What does John Nielsen say about self-driving cars?
options: A) Their drivers would feel safe after getting used to the automatic devices.
B) They would be unpopular with drivers who only trust their own skills.
C) Their increased comfort levels have boosted their sales.
D) They are not actually as safe as automakers advertise.

explain.定位:
He also believes they will be more likely to trust self-driving cars as they become more
familiar with features such as automatic braking or parking.
他还认为，随着司机对自动刹车、自动泊车这类功能越来越熟悉，他们会更愿意信任自动驾
驶汽车。
explain.信号:
人名 + believes 引出本人观点。答案句紧跟在人名 John Nielsen 之后，由 He also
believes（他还认为）这一观点标志词领起——专家亲口说的预测，正是态度观点题要锁定
的答案句。
explain.替换:
more likely to trust self-driving cars ↔ would feel safe
『更愿信任』等值于『会觉得安全』
as they become more familiar with features such as automatic braking or parking ↔
after getting used to the automatic devices
『越来越熟悉这些功能』改写为『习惯了这些自动装置之后』
explain.排除:
B) 张冠李戴
only trust their own skills 搬了原文第三段 they trust their own driving skills 的原词，
但那是『被调查的司机』说的、不是 Nielsen 说的；且 Nielsen 的观点恰恰相反——他认
为司机高估了自己。把别人的话安到 Nielsen 头上，张冠李戴。
借用原文：those surveyed by AAA say they trust their own driving skills
C) 原词陷阱
increased comfort levels have boosted their sales 借用了原文末段 the comfort level
will increase 的原词 comfort level，但原文只说『舒适接受度会提升』，从没说提升了销
量（sales 全文未提），是把熟词嫁接到一个录音没说的因果上，无中生有。
借用原文：He estimated that the "comfort level" will increase considerably in five to ten years.
D) 与原文相反
not actually as safe as automakers advertise（其实没厂商宣传的那么安全）是个看空自
动驾驶的负面判断，但 Nielsen 的态度是看好——他认为司机会越来越信任这种车，极性正
好相反，且原文从没出现『没宣传得安全』这层意思。
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1 One dog has been killed and multiple dogs have been injured by a snowmobile driver in what appears
to be an intentional attack on competitors in the Iditarod Race in Alaska.
一名雪地摩托车驾驶员杀死了一只狗，并导致多只狗受伤，这似乎是对阿拉斯加Iditarod比赛参赛者的蓄
意攻击。
2 Aliy Zirkle was the first to report an attack. A snowmobile driver had repeatedly attempted to harm
her and her team, and one of Zirkle's dogs had received a non-life-threatening injury. Zirkle reported the
attack when she arrived in Nulato, Alaska, in the early hours of the morning. Then Jeff King, a four-
time champion, reported a similar attack. His team was hit by a snowmobile driver, injuring several dogs
and killing a 3-year-old male dog.
Aliy Zirkle是第一个报告遭到袭击的人。一名雪地摩托车驾驶员曾多次试图伤害她和她的狗队,Zirkle的一
只狗受了非致命伤。Zirkle在凌晨抵达阿拉斯加Nulato时报告了这次袭击。随后,四届冠军Jeff King报告了
类似的袭击。他的狗队被一名雪地摩托车驾驶员撞击,导致几只狗受伤,一只3岁的雄性犬死亡。
3 Reporter Zachariah Hughes says that neither King nor Zirkle was injured. Although this incident very
much alters the race of the two participants competing for a win, both are going to continue on their
way toward the finishing line. Alaska State Troopers released a statement saying they've arrested Arnold
Demoski, 26. He faces trial on several charges.
记者Zachariah Hughes称King和Zirkle均未受伤。尽管这一事件极大地改变了这两名争夺胜利的参赛者
的比赛进程,但两人都将继续前往终点线。阿拉斯加州警方发布声明称他们已逮捕26岁的Arnold
Demoski。他将面临多项指控的审判。

questions.stem: What is the news report mainly about?
options: A) Thefts of snowmobile dogs in Alaska.
B) A series of injuries to snowmobile drivers.
C) Attacks on some Iditarod Race competitors.
D) A serious accident in the Alaska sports event.

explain.定位:
One dog has been killed and multiple dogs have been injured by a snowmobile driver in what
appears to be an intentional attack on competitors in the Iditarod Race in Alaska.
一名雪地摩托驾驶者撞死了一只狗、撞伤了多只狗，这看起来是对阿拉斯加 Iditarod 比赛
参赛者的一次蓄意攻击。
explain.信号:
导语首句即总起。新闻第一句 in what appears to be an intentional attack on
competitors in the Iditarod Race 就是导语总起句，一句话点明核心事件是"对参赛者的蓄
意攻击"，主旨题的落点就在这种开篇总起句上。
explain.替换:
an intentional attack on competitors in the Iditarod Race ↔
Attacks on some Iditarod Race competitors
几乎同词，attack=Attacks
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
选项 Thefts of snowmobile dogs in Alaska 把原文里真实出现的 dog、snowmobile、
Alaska 拼在一起，却把性质偷换成 Thefts\(盗窃\)；原文是撞死撞伤狗的攻击，从未提偷
狗，听到 dog 就奔这项就中招了。
借用原文：One dog has been killed and multiple dogs have been injured by a snowmobile driver
B) 张冠李戴
选项 A series of injuries to snowmobile drivers 借用原文 injured/snowmobile driver
的原词，但说的是"雪地摩托司机受伤"——原文受伤的是参赛者的狗，司机是施害方而非受
害方；且"受伤"只是攻击的结果细节，不是整件事的定性。
借用原文：multiple dogs have been injured by a snowmobile driver
D) 偷换概念
选项 A serious accident in the Alaska sports event 用 Alaska、event 等原文气味的词，
却把事件定性成 accident\(意外事故\)；原文明确说 what appears to be an intentional
attack\(蓄意攻击\)，accident 与 intentional 性质相反，把"故意"说成"意外"。
借用原文：what appears to be an intentional attack

questions.stem: What do we learn about Jeff King?
options: A) He stayed behind to look after his injured dogs.
B) He has won the Alaska Iditarod Race four times.
C) He received a minor injury in the Iditarod Race.
D) He has quit the competition in Alaska for good.

explain.定位:
Then Jeff King, a four-time champion, reported a similar attack.
随后，四度夺冠的 Jeff King 也报告了一起类似的攻击。
explain.信号:
人名后紧跟的同位语身份说明。锁定人名 Jeff King 后，紧跟其后的同位语 a four-time
champion 就是关于他最直接的身份信息；细节题的落点常在人名后紧贴的修饰说明上。
explain.替换:
a four-time champion ↔ He has won the Alaska Iditarod Race four times
名词头衔展开成完整句
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
选项 He stayed behind to look after his injured dogs 借用原文 injured/dog 的原词，
但原文明确说 both are going to continue on their way toward the finishing line\(两人
都继续奔向终点\)，他并没有留下来；"留下照看伤狗"是录音从未说过的虚构。
借用原文：injuring several dogs and killing a 3-year-old male dog
C) 张冠李戴
选项 He received a minor injury in the Iditarod Race 盗用原文 injury 一词，但原文受伤
的是狗\(injuring several dogs\)，且 neither King nor Zirkle was injured 明说 King 本人
没有受伤；把"狗受伤"偷换成"他受轻伤"。
借用原文：neither King nor Zirkle was injured
D) 与原文相反
选项 He has quit the competition in Alaska for good 说他永久退赛，与原文 both are
going to continue on their way toward the finishing line\(都将继续奔向终点\)极性完全
相反；competition/Alaska 是原文气味词，但 quit 与 continue 正好反过来。
借用原文：both are going to continue on their way toward the finishing line

questions.stem: What happened to the tour boat sailing off the Nicaraguan coast?
options: A) It sank into the sea due to overloading.
B) It ran into Nicaragua's Big Corn Island.
C) It disappeared between two large islands.
D) It turned over because of strong winds.

explain.定位:
A tour boat turned over off the coast of Nicaragua, killing at least 13 people and leaving more
passengers missing, officials said.
一艘游船在尼加拉瓜海岸附近翻覆，造成至少 13 人死亡、更多乘客失踪，官方表示。
explain.信号:
开篇首句即点事件核心。新闻报道惯例是第一句话就把核心事件交代清楚，A tour boat
turned over off the coast of Nicaragua 正是这则新闻的导语，turned over（翻覆）就是
船出事的方式，是本题答案信号。
explain.替换:
A tour boat turned over ↔ It turned over
原句动词直接对应
because of bad weather and strong winds ↔ because of strong winds
原因句同义保留
explain.排除:
A) 未提及
录音明确说原因是 strong winds，从未提到 overloading（超载）。sank into the sea
due to overloading 把翻船编成『因超载而沉』，原因纯属杜撰，且 sank（沉没）也不是
录音说的 turned over（翻覆）。
B) 原词陷阱
录音确实念到 Big Corn Island，但原文是说船在两岛之间『航行』、在较大那座岛附近翻
覆，并非『撞上』Big Corn Island。ran into Nicaragua's Big Corn Island 借这个真出现
过的岛名，把『在附近翻』偷换成『撞岛』。
借用原文：traveling between Nicaragua's Big Corn Island and Little Corn Island, turned over
Saturday near the larger island
C) 偷换概念
录音说的是船在 Big Corn Island and Little Corn Island 之间航行后翻覆，而非
disappeared between two large islands（在两大岛间消失）。disappeared 是录音没有
的；况且原文里一大一小（Little/larger island），并非两座都是 large。
借用原文：traveling between Nicaragua's Big Corn Island and Little Corn Island, turned over
Saturday near the larger island

这艘船载有 32 人——25 名哥斯达黎加人、4 名美国人和 3 名尼加拉瓜人。
explain.信号:
carrying与题干同词，紧跟总数。录音 The boat was carrying 32 people 里的 carrying
与题干 carrying 同词，其后紧跟的 32 就是总数；破折号后的 25/4/3 是分国籍拆分，是干
扰数字。
explain.替换:
The boat was carrying 32 people ↔ 32.

总人数。13. 盗用了这个真出现过的数字，但答非所问。

B) 原词陷阱
录音 25 Costa Ricans 说的是 25 名哥斯达黎加籍乘客，只是船上某一国籍的人数，并非载
客总数。25. 套用了这个分项数字来冒充总数。
借用原文：25 Costa Ricans
C) 未提及

字就能直接排除。

options: A) He has helped with the rescue effort.
B) He is being investigated by the police.
C) He was drowned with the passengers.
D) He is among those people missing.

explain.定位:

末段交代船主结局，being investigated是落点。录音先说船主 rescued, including the
tour boat's owner, Hilario Blandon 获救，再到末段 are being investigated for
unintentional murder，落点是最后这句『正在接受调查』——后文交代的处境才是问『关
于船主我们知道什么』的完整答案。

are being investigated for unintentional murder ↔ He is being investigated by the police
调查动作直接对应
according to police ↔ by the police
施动者police对应

A) 原词陷阱
录音说船主是被救者之一 an unspecified number of people were rescued, including
the tour boat's owner，并非去『帮助救援』。helped with the rescue effort 借了
rescue 这个真出现的词，把『被救』篡改成『参与救援』。
借用原文：an unspecified number of people were rescued, including the tour boat's owner,
Hilario Blandon
C) 与原文相反
录音明说船主在获救名单里 rescued, including the tour boat's owner，遇难的 13 人是哥
斯达黎加乘客。was drowned with the passengers 与原文相反，把获救者说成与乘客一
同溺亡。
借用原文：rescued, including the tour boat's owner, Hilario Blandon
D) 张冠李戴
录音里 missing（失踪）指的是 Some passengers remain missing 部分乘客，而船主已
明确获救并被捕。among those people missing 把『失踪乘客』这个真概念安到船主头
上，张冠李戴。

questions.stem: What does the man say about Americans?
options: A) They are keen on high technology.
B) They are poor at technology skills.
C) They often listen to National Public Radio.
D) They feel superior in science and technology.

explain.定位:

naming a file on a computer, using a link on a webpage, or just texting someone.
我们先从坏消息说起：美国人在技术技能上糟透了——发邮件、给电脑文件命名、点开网页
链接，甚至只是给别人发条短信都不行。
explain.信号:
bad news 定调 + terrible 直接评价。男士一开口就用 the bad news 给整段定了负面调
子，紧接着 Americans are terrible at technology skills 直接给出对美国人的评价词
terrible，这种“直接亮明褒贬”的句子就是细节评价题的答案句。

questions.stem: What do we learn from the conversation about American high school education?
options: A) It is undergoing a drastic reform.
B) It lays emphasis on creative thinking.
C) It has much room for improvement.

explain.定位:
What does that tell us about our education system? Well, it tells us that we need to think about
the preparedness of our students as they are leaving high school.
这告诉了我们关于教育体系的什么呢？嗯，它告诉我们，必须好好考虑学生离开高中时的准
备程度（够不够）。

we need to… 的待改进语气定调。男士先自问 What does that tell us about our

“有很多事要做” = 有改进空间

questions.stem: What do we learn from the talk about wild carrots?
options: D) They come from Central Africa.

explain.定位:
With wild carrots, the roots are white, small and skinny, so you'd have to pick a lot of wild

野胡萝卜的根又白又小又细，所以你得采很多野胡萝卜才够吃。

questions.stem: What does the speaker say about carrots in the late 1500s?
options: A) They turned from white to purple in color.
B) They became popular on the world market.
C) They became an important food for humans.
D) They began to look like modern-day carrots.

explain.定位:
Then, in the late 1500s, food scientists in the Netherlands cultivated large, straight, sweet, red
carrots like the ones we eat today.
然后，在16世纪晚期，荷兰的食品科学家培育出了又大又直又甜的红胡萝卜，就像我们今天
吃的这种。
explain.信号:
时间锚 in the late 1500s 引出的句子。录音里 in the late 1500s 这个时间词一出现，紧
跟的整句就是本题答案句；句末 like the ones we eat today（像我们今天吃的）是定调的
关键信号，点明此时已接近现代样子。
explain.替换:
large, straight, sweet, red carrots like the ones we eat today ↔
They began to look like modern-day carrots.
today 概括为 modern-day

"从白变紫"确实在录音里——但发生在 Around 800 AD 的 a purple carrot，不是 the late

的年代上，是典型的时间张冠李戴。
借用原文：Around 800 AD, people in Central Asia managed to develop a new kind of carrot—a
purple carrot

"国际市场流行"的影子来自 a purple carrot—that attracted more interest from

并非选项 became popular on the world market 所说的"在世界市场流行"，既错了年代又
拔高了程度。
借用原文：a purple carrot—that attracted more interest from international traders

"成为人类重要食物"对应的是录音第4段 carrots got their biggest boost during the two

donkeys and pigs, and didn't eat them themselves（人们当时主要喂牲口、自己不

questions.stem: Why did people turn to carrots for food during the two world wars?
options: A) They were found quite nutritious.
B) There were serious food shortages.
C) People discovered their medicinal value.
D) Farm machines helped lower their prices.

explain.定位:
But carrots got their biggest boost during the two world wars, when food shortages forced
people to eat them, and governments told everyone how healthy carrots were.
但胡萝卜在两次世界大战期间获得了最大的推动，当时粮食短缺迫使人们吃它，政府也告诉
大家胡萝卜有多健康。

借用原文：In the 1600s, people in China used carrots as medicine

questions.stem: What was one particular convenience Katherine loved about Facebook?

B) She could call up her family whenever she liked

questions.stem: How did Katherine feel when her classmates added her as a Facebook friend?
options: A) She liked to inform her friends about her success.
B) She enjoyed reading her friends' status updates.
C) She felt quite popular among them.
D) She felt she was a teenager again.

explain.定位:
At first, this didn't bother her. She loved learning about the success of people she knew when
she was just a teenager. She loved finding out people were getting married, having babies,
and traveling.
起初这并没让她困扰。她喜欢了解那些自己少年时认识的人如今取得了什么成就，喜欢得知
大家结婚、生子、四处旅行的近况。

——她享受的是"了解别人的近况成就"。

She loved learning about the success of people she knew ↔
She enjoyed reading her friends' status updates.

里的"success"，但方向反了：原文是她"了解别人的成就"，A 却说她"向朋友炫耀自己的成

King Charles III of Spain sent Washington a male donkey ↔ It was brought over from Spain.

了人名却把"被赠予"偷换成"被华盛顿买下"，原文是 as a gift(礼物)而非购买。
借用原文：sent Washington a male donkey as a gift

questions.passage:
Team spirit

A) Teams have become the basic building blocks of organizations. Recruitment advertisements routinely call for "team players". Business schools grade their students in part on their performance in group projects. Office managers knock down walls to encourage team building. Teams are as old as civilization, of course: even Jesus had 12 co-workers. But a new report by Deloitte, "Global Human Capital Trends", based on a survey of more than 7,000 executives in over 130 countries, suggests that the fashion for teamwork has reached a new high. Almost half of those surveyed said their companies were either in the middle of restructuring or about to embark on(开始) it; and for the most part, restructuring meant putting more emphasis on teams.

B) Companies are abandoning conventional functional departments and organising employees into cross-disciplinary teams that focus on particular products, problems or customers. These teams are gaining more power to run their own affairs. They are also spending more time working with each other rather than reporting upwards. Deloitte argues that a new organisational form is on the rise: a network of teams is replacing the conventional hierarchy(等级体制).

C) The fashion for teams is driven by a sense that the old way of organising people is too rigid for both the modern marketplace and the expectations of employees. Technological innovation places greater value on agility(灵活性). John Chambers, chairman of Cisco Systems Inc., a worldwide leader in electronics products, says that "we compete against market transitions(过渡), not competitors. Product transitions used to take five or seven years; now they take one or two." Digital technology also makes it easier for people to co-ordinate their activities without resorting to hierarchy. The "millennials"(千禧一代) who will soon make up half the workforce in rich countries were raised from nursery school onwards to work in groups.

D) The fashion for teams is also spreading from the usual corporate suspects (such as GE and IBM) to some more unusual ones. The Cleveland Clinic, a hospital operator, has reorganised its medical staff into teams to focus on particular treatment areas; consultants, nurses and others collaborate closely instead of being separated by speciality(专业) and rank. The US Army has gone the same way. In his book, Team of Teams, General Stanley McChrystal describes how the army's hierarchical structure hindered its operations during the early stages of the Iraq war. His solution was to learn something from the rebels it was fighting: decentralising authority to self-organising teams.

E) A good rule of thumb is that as soon as generals and hospital administrators jump on a management bandwagon, it is time to ask questions. Leigh Thompson of Kellogg School of Management in Illinois warns that, "Teams are not always the answer—teams may provide insight, creativity and knowledge in a way that a person working independently cannot; but teamwork may also lead to confusion, delay and poor decision-making." The late Richard Hackman of Harvard University once argued, "I have no question that when you have a team, the possibility exists that it will generate magic, producing something extraordinary… But don't count on it."

F) Hackman (who died in 2013) noted that teams are hindered by problems of co-ordination and motivation that chip away at the benefits of collaboration. High-flyers forced to work in teams may be undervalued and free-riders empowered. Group-think may be unavoidable. In a study of 120 teams of senior executives, he discovered that less than 10% of their supposed members agreed on who exactly was on the team. If it is hard enough to define a team's membership, agreeing on its purpose is harder still.

G) Profound changes in the workforce are making teams trickier to manage. Teams work best if their members have a strong common culture. This is hard to achieve when, as is now the case in many big firms, a large proportion of staff are temporary contractors. Teamwork improves with time: America's National Transportation Safety Board found that 73% of the incidents in its civil-aviation database occurred on a crew's first day of flying together. However, as Amy Edmondson of Harvard points out, organisations increasingly use "team" as a verb rather than a noun: they form teams for specific purposes and then quickly disband them.

H) The least that can be concluded from this research is that companies need to think harder about managing teams. They need to rid their minds of sentimentalism(感情用事): the most successful teams have leaders who are able to set an overall direction and take immediate action. They need to keep teams small and focused: giving in to pressure to be more "inclusive" is a guarantee of dysfunction. Jeff Bezos, Amazon's boss, says that "If I see more than two pizzas for lunch, the team is too big." They need to immunize teams against group-think: Hackman argued that the best ones contain "deviants"(离经叛道者) who are willing to do something that may be upsetting to others.

I) A new study of 12,000 workers in 17 countries by Steelcase, a furniture-maker which also does consulting, finds that the best way to ensure employees are "engaged" is to give them more control over where and how they do their work―which may mean liberating them from having to do everything in collaboration with others.

J) However, organisations need to learn something bigger than how to manage teams better: they need to be in the habit of asking themselves whether teams are the best tools for the job. Teambuilding skills are in short supply: Deloitte reports that only 12% of the executives they contacted feel they understand the way people work together in networks and only 21% feel confident in their ability to build cross-functional teams. Loosely managed teams can become hotbeds of distraction―employees routinely complain that they can't get their work done because they are forced to spend too much time in meetings or compelled to work in noisy offices. Even in the age of open-plan offices and social networks some work is best left to the individual.

questions.stem: Product transitions take much less time now than in the past.
questions.passage:
Team spirit

A) Teams have become the basic building blocks of organizations. Recruitment advertisements routinely call for "team players". Business schools grade their students in part on their performance in group projects. Office managers knock down walls to encourage team building. Teams are as old as civilization, of course: even Jesus had 12 co-workers. But a new report by Deloitte, "Global Human Capital Trends", based on a survey of more than 7,000 executives in over 130 countries, suggests that the fashion for teamwork has reached a new high. Almost half of those surveyed said their companies were either in the middle of restructuring or about to embark on(开始) it; and for the most part, restructuring meant putting more emphasis on teams.

B) Companies are abandoning conventional functional departments and organising employees into cross-disciplinary teams that focus on particular products, problems or customers. These teams are gaining more power to run their own affairs. They are also spending more time working with each other rather than reporting upwards. Deloitte argues that a new organisational form is on the rise: a network of teams is replacing the conventional hierarchy(等级体制).

C) The fashion for teams is driven by a sense that the old way of organising people is too rigid for both the modern marketplace and the expectations of employees. Technological innovation places greater value on agility(灵活性). John Chambers, chairman of Cisco Systems Inc., a worldwide leader in electronics products, says that "we compete against market transitions(过渡), not competitors. Product transitions used to take five or seven years; now they take one or two." Digital technology also makes it easier for people to co-ordinate their activities without resorting to hierarchy. The "millennials"(千禧一代) who will soon make up half the workforce in rich countries were raised from nursery school onwards to work in groups.

D) The fashion for teams is also spreading from the usual corporate suspects (such as GE and IBM) to some more unusual ones. The Cleveland Clinic, a hospital operator, has reorganised its medical staff into teams to focus on particular treatment areas; consultants, nurses and others collaborate closely instead of being separated by speciality(专业) and rank. The US Army has gone the same way. In his book, Team of Teams, General Stanley McChrystal describes how the army's hierarchical structure hindered its operations during the early stages of the Iraq war. His solution was to learn something from the rebels it was fighting: decentralising authority to self-organising teams.

E) A good rule of thumb is that as soon as generals and hospital administrators jump on a management bandwagon, it is time to ask questions. Leigh Thompson of Kellogg School of Management in Illinois warns that, "Teams are not always the answer—teams may provide insight, creativity and knowledge in a way that a person working independently cannot; but teamwork may also lead to confusion, delay and poor decision-making." The late Richard Hackman of Harvard University once argued, "I have no question that when you have a team, the possibility exists that it will generate magic, producing something extraordinary… But don't count on it."

F) Hackman (who died in 2013) noted that teams are hindered by problems of co-ordination and motivation that chip away at the benefits of collaboration. High-flyers forced to work in teams may be undervalued and free-riders empowered. Group-think may be unavoidable. In a study of 120 teams of senior executives, he discovered that less than 10% of their supposed members agreed on who exactly was on the team. If it is hard enough to define a team's membership, agreeing on its purpose is harder still.

G) Profound changes in the workforce are making teams trickier to manage. Teams work best if their members have a strong common culture. This is hard to achieve when, as is now the case in many big firms, a large proportion of staff are temporary contractors. Teamwork improves with time: America's National Transportation Safety Board found that 73% of the incidents in its civil-aviation database occurred on a crew's first day of flying together. However, as Amy Edmondson of Harvard points out, organisations increasingly use "team" as a verb rather than a noun: they form teams for specific purposes and then quickly disband them.

H) The least that can be concluded from this research is that companies need to think harder about managing teams. They need to rid their minds of sentimentalism(感情用事): the most successful teams have leaders who are able to set an overall direction and take immediate action. They need to keep teams small and focused: giving in to pressure to be more "inclusive" is a guarantee of dysfunction. Jeff Bezos, Amazon's boss, says that "If I see more than two pizzas for lunch, the team is too big." They need to immunize teams against group-think: Hackman argued that the best ones contain "deviants"(离经叛道者) who are willing to do something that may be upsetting to others.

I) A new study of 12,000 workers in 17 countries by Steelcase, a furniture-maker which also does consulting, finds that the best way to ensure employees are "engaged" is to give them more control over where and how they do their work―which may mean liberating them from having to do everything in collaboration with others.

J) However, organisations need to learn something bigger than how to manage teams better: they need to be in the habit of asking themselves whether teams are the best tools for the job. Teambuilding skills are in short supply: Deloitte reports that only 12% of the executives they contacted feel they understand the way people work together in networks and only 21% feel confident in their ability to build cross-functional teams. Loosely managed teams can become hotbeds of distraction―employees routinely complain that they can't get their work done because they are forced to spend too much time in meetings or compelled to work in noisy offices. Even in the age of open-plan offices and social networks some work is best left to the individual.

Shoppers in the UK are spending less money on toilet paper to save money, research has shown.

Penny-pinching UK consumers choose cheaper products from discounters such as Aldi and Lidl rather than luxury alternatives.

This has wiped 6% off the value of the soft tissue paper market in the UK. It has shrunk from £1.19 billion in 2011 to £1.12 billion in 2015, according to a new report from market research company Mintel. Furthermore, the future of the market looks far from rosy, with sales expected to fall further to £1.11 billion in 2016.

In the last year alone, despite an increase in the UK population and a subsequent rise in the number of households, sales of toilet paper fell by 2%, with the average household reducing their toilet roll spending from £43 in 2014 to £41 in 2015.

Overall, almost three in five people say they try to limit their usage of paper—including facial tissue and kitchen roll―to save money. "Strength, softness and thickness remain the leading indicators of toilet paper quality, with just a small proportion of consumers preferring more luxurious alternatives, such as those with flower patterns or perfume," said Mintel analyst Jack Duckett. "These extra features are deemed unnecessary by the majority of shoppers, which probably reflects how these types of products are typically more expensive than regular toilet paper, even when on special offer."

While consumers are spending less on toilet paper, they remain fussy—in theory at least—when it comes to paper quality. Top of Britons' toilet paper wish list is softness (57%) followed by strength (45%) and thickness (36%).

One in 10 buyers rank toilet rolls made from recycled paper among their top considerations, highlighting how overall the environment is much less of a consideration for shoppers than product quality. questions.passage:
"One of the reasons I find this topic very interesting is because my mom was a smoker when I was younger," says Lindson-Hawley, who studies tobacco and health at the University of Oxford.

By studying about 700 adult smokers, she found out that her mom quit the right way—by stopping abruptly and completely.

In her study, participants were randomly(随机地) assigned to two groups. One had to quit abruptly on a given day, going from about a pack a day to zero. The other cut down gradually over the course of two weeks. People in both groups used nicotine(尼古丁) patches before they quit, in addition to a second form of nicotine replacement, like gum or spray. They also had talk therapy with a nurse before and after quit day.

Six months out, more people who had quit abruptly had stuck with it—more than one-fifth of them, compared to about one-seventh in the other group. Although these numbers appear low, it is much higher than if people try without support.

And the quit rates were particularly convincing given that before the study started, most of the people had said they'd rather cut down gradually before quitting. "If you're training for a marathon, you wouldn't expect to turn up and just be able to run it. And I think people see that for smoking as well. They think, 'Well, if I gradually reduce, it's like practice,'" says Lindson-Hawley. But that wasn't the case. Instead of giving people practice, the gradual reduction likely gave them cravings(瘾) and withdrawal symptoms before they even reached quit day, which could be why fewer people in that group actually made it to that point. "Regardless of your stated preference, if you're ready to quit, quitting abruptly is more effective," says Dr. Gabriela Ferreira. "When you can quote a specific number like a fifth of the patients were able to quit, that's compelling. It gives them the encouragement, I think, to really go for it," Ferreira says.

People rarely manage to quit the first time they try. But at least, she says, they can maximize the odds of success.

questions.passage:
"One of the reasons I find this topic very interesting is because my mom was a smoker when I was younger," says Lindson-Hawley, who studies tobacco and health at the University of Oxford.

By studying about 700 adult smokers, she found out that her mom quit the right way—by stopping abruptly and completely.

In her study, participants were randomly(随机地) assigned to two groups. One had to quit abruptly on a given day, going from about a pack a day to zero. The other cut down gradually over the course of two weeks. People in both groups used nicotine(尼古丁) patches before they quit, in addition to a second form of nicotine replacement, like gum or spray. They also had talk therapy with a nurse before and after quit day.

Six months out, more people who had quit abruptly had stuck with it—more than one-fifth of them, compared to about one-seventh in the other group. Although these numbers appear low, it is much higher than if people try without support.

And the quit rates were particularly convincing given that before the study started, most of the people had said they'd rather cut down gradually before quitting. "If you're training for a marathon, you wouldn't expect to turn up and just be able to run it. And I think people see that for smoking as well. They think, 'Well, if I gradually reduce, it's like practice,'" says Lindson-Hawley. But that wasn't the case. Instead of giving people practice, the gradual reduction likely gave them cravings(瘾) and withdrawal symptoms before they even reached quit day, which could be why fewer people in that group actually made it to that point. "Regardless of your stated preference, if you're ready to quit, quitting abruptly is more effective," says Dr. Gabriela Ferreira. "When you can quote a specific number like a fifth of the patients were able to quit, that's compelling. It gives them the encouragement, I think, to really go for it," Ferreira says.

People rarely manage to quit the first time they try. But at least, she says, they can maximize the odds of success.
